messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When he first describes what happened, Arun does not tell it as a single clean story. He is a 51-year-old married tax inspector, a careful, orderly man who is used to evidence and sequence, yet when he speaks about the abuse by a former romantic partner, the account comes in jagged sections. He remembers her face changing in an instant during arguments, the atmosphere in the apartment becoming charged and unreadable, and the particular terror of not knowing when a conversation would turn. What stands out most clearly is the sense of unpredictability: a normal evening could become dangerous without warning. He recalls being shoved hard enough to lose balance, struck during confrontations, and cornered in rooms where he felt trapped and watched for the next movement. Other parts will not come. He says there are stretches he has tried repeatedly to recover but cannot, as if pieces of the event were cut out altogether. At other times fragments force themselves in without invitation—a flash of her arm moving toward him, the pressure of bracing himself, the shock of realizing that someone he loved had become someone he feared.

In the weeks after leaving that relationship, Arun tried to carry on as if the matter were over. He went to work, reviewed filings, met with taxpayers, and told himself that because he was no longer living with her he should be able to move on. Instead, the memories began to intrude in ways that felt humiliating and beyond his control. A fragment would break into his mind while he was sitting at his desk, or while waiting for an elevator, and then vanish before he could make sense of it. He found this especially unnerving because he could not summon the memory deliberately in a complete form, no matter how hard he tried. The pieces came when they wanted. He came to dread that loss of control almost as much as the original violence.

Certain states now unsettle him immediately. When he is very tired at the end of a long workday, he notices himself becoming sharply uneasy, as if exhaustion leaves him exposed. Ordinary physical discomfort can do the same. If his collar feels tight, if a chair is awkward, if he is stuck too long in a warm conference room, his body seems to register danger before his mind has caught up. Unpredictable situations are particularly difficult. At work he can tolerate routine audits and scheduled meetings, but if a taxpayer arrives angry without an appointment, or a supervisor changes plans suddenly and asks him to join an unscripted discussion, he feels a jolt of alarm that seems wildly out of proportion to what is happening. He knows, even in the moment, that nothing is actually wrong, yet he reacts as if he is in immediate danger.

That sense of danger has crept into the physical way he moves through the world. In restaurants, training rooms, and waiting areas, Arun looks first for a seat where his back can rest against a wall and he can see the room. If none is available, he remains tense and distracted, unable to follow conversation fully. In the office he has shifted how he arranges himself during meetings, choosing chairs at the perimeter when he can do so without drawing attention. Walking from the parking garage into the government building, he often checks behind him more than once, scanning to see whether anyone is following. He feels embarrassed by this, especially because his work depends on appearing composed and authoritative, but the checking has become automatic enough that he sometimes notices it only after he has already turned around.

What distresses Arun most is what the abuse has come to mean about him and about other people. He had trusted this partner intimately, and he is certain he was betrayed. He speaks of that betrayal not abstractly but with injury and disbelief: the person who should have cared for him instead used his closeness to hurt him. Since then, he has had periods when he feels less like a person than like something handled and positioned by someone else, as if his own subjectivity had been stripped away. He also speaks bleakly about the future. Nothing good can happen to me anymore, he says flatly, not as melodrama but as a conclusion he has repeated to himself often enough that it now feels factual.

His marriage has been affected not by any lack of love for his wife, but by the narrowing of his world. He avoids many spontaneous outings because he cannot tolerate not knowing what the setting will be like. When he is exhausted, he becomes withdrawn rather than talkative because he knows how easily he startles and how quickly his mind fills with fragments he does not want. Over time his wife has noticed that he studies rooms on entry, chooses the same protected seat, and seems to disappear into himself when physically uncomfortable or overtired.

He sought help after a recent week at work in which several unexpected schedule changes left him feeling constantly on edge. By the time he got home each evening he was exhausted, and with the exhaustion came more intrusive fragments and more scanning. What finally frightened him was not one dramatic incident but the realization that he was organizing more and more of his life around feeling unsafe. Sitting in the intake session, with his chair angled so he could see the door, Arun said he wants some possibility that life might feel human again. What he fears most is that this is permanent: that he will always be the man who cannot trust, cannot relax, and cannot believe anything good is still ahead.
